summary:
We developed BASELINE, a web app that helps astronauts answer one question about their health readings: "Is this space, or is this me?"

In space, normal moves: resting core temperature rises about 1 °C over the first ~75 days (Stahn et al. 2017), so Earth limits and pre-launch values alone give wrong answers.

BASELINE compares each daily reading (core temperature, resting heart rate, sleep and mood) with what is normal for this astronaut on this mission day. It gives one of four plain statuses (Normal for you, Keep an eye on it, Tell your medical officer, No data), explains why, shows how sure it is, and drafts an SBAR note for the crew medical officer.

What makes it different: it combines a research-based expected change with the size learned from the astronaut's own data, instead of only following recent readings. When adaptation and a real problem look the same, it says "can't tell" rather than "normal". And we tested it openly: on a slow unexplained drift, a "last 14 days" baseline caught 0 of 9 problem days; BASELINE caught 9 of 9.

All data is simulated; it is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

BASELINE is a web app that helps an astronaut on a long mission understand their own health readings: "Is this space, or is this me?" In space the body changes — resting core temperature rises about 1 °C over the first ~75 days (Stahn et al. 2017, 11 ISS astronauts) — so Earth limits miss changes that are large for one person, and comparing only with pre-launch values raises weeks of false alarms.

For four daily measures (core temperature, resting heart rate, sleep, mood), BASELINE asks five questions in order:

1. Is there a usable reading?

2. Is it different from her normal before launch?

3. Is it still different after the expected space change?

4. Has it lasted more than one day (2 of the last 3 days)?

5. Is it past a general Earth medical limit (shown for context)?

The answer is one of four plain statuses — Normal for you, Keep an eye on it, Tell your medical officer, No data — with a confidence level (High / Medium / Low, always with the reason) and a "Why this result?" explanation. When readings stay unusual, BASELINE drafts an SBAR note (Situation, Background, Assessment, Request) for the crew medical officer, which the astronaut reviews, edits, copies or downloads.

The app has four screens: Today (overall status, four measure cards, what needs attention, data quality, daily check-in), Over time (a chart of the whole mission), Note to doctor, and Science & sources. A 2-minute guided demo walks through the key moments.

BENEFITS

- Fewer false alarms on changes that are expected in space.

- Catches changes that are unusual for this person even when they stay below Earth limits.

- Missing data is never shown as normal; confidence drops when readings are missing.

- A ready, structured handoff for the crew medical officer instead of raw numbers.

INTENDED IMPACT

On long missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays mean crews must interpret their own data on board. BASELINE is a decision-support prototype for that situation: it helps the crew notice what matters, explains why, and supports — never replaces — the crew medical officer.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE (WHAT IS DIFFERENT)

- It combines a research-based expected change with the size learned from the astronaut's own in-flight data, instead of only following recent readings. Example: the same 37.6 °C reading is "Keep an eye on it" on day 4 but "Normal for you" on day 90.

- A "can't tell" safeguard: when normal adaptation and a real problem look the same, it says so instead of calling the reading normal.

- We tested it against other methods and show the results, including weak spots. The same engine runs on 8 simulated astronauts who adapt more, less, faster or not at all, or drift slowly. On a slow unexplained drift, a "last 14 days" baseline caught 0 of 9 problem days and BASELINE caught 9 of 9. Our first version missed a slow drift in 15 of 20 simulated runs; after adding the safeguard it missed 0 of 20. Fast or strong adapters still get extra alerts, and the app shows this openly.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

React 19 and TypeScript, built with Vite; charts with Recharts; 132 automated tests with Vitest; hosted on Vercel; source code on GitHub (https://github.com/sridharan-71/baseline-space-health). It runs entirely in the browser — no backend, no database, no hardware. Daily check-ins are saved only in the browser. The scientific engine is kept separate from the user interface, and all research numbers live in one place in the code.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: every rule is labelled Research, Clinical reference or Design assumption. Only core temperature has a research-based space model; heart rate, sleep and mood are compared with the astronaut's own history, and the app says so.

- No combined health score: each measure is judged on its own, so one warning can never be averaged away.

- Safety: BASELINE never diagnoses, never suggests medicine and never replaces the crew medical officer.

- Limits we state openly: all data is simulated (fictional astronaut Cmdr. Asha Rao); thresholds are prototype choices, not clinically validated; the temperature model comes from a small study.

- Clarity: plain-language statuses, icons and words as well as colour, and a layout that works on desktop and phone.

USE OF AI

Code, documentation and slide text were written with Anthropic's Claude (an AI assistant) under our team's direction. We chose the idea, scope, scientific sources and rules, and reviewed and tested the result. Screenshots are of our own app.
